crossed.name: Sternocleidomastoid & scalenes
crossed.pattern: Upper crossed · anterior · tight, facilitated (type I postural) → stretch
crossed.exercise: Stretch, seated: the opposite hand pins the clavicle; tuck the chin and glide the head straight back, side-bend away from the tight side, then rotate either way into the pull. Hold 15-20 s, both sides

crossed.name: Pectoralis major (upper fibers) & pectoralis minor
crossed.pattern: Upper crossed · anterior · tight, facilitated (type I postural) → stretch
crossed.exercise: Stretch: hands on a door frame at about nose height, elbows near 90°, lean the chest forward through the doorway. Hold 30-45 s, then repeat with the hands 6 inches higher

crossed.name: Upper trapezius
crossed.pattern: Upper crossed · posterior · tight, facilitated (type I postural) → stretch
crossed.exercise: Stretch: the opposite hand stabilizes the clavicle and 1st rib; flex the neck, side-bend AWAY and rotate TOWARD the tight side, into the barrier. Hold 15-20 s, both sides

crossed.name: Levator scapulae
crossed.pattern: Upper crossed · posterior · tight, facilitated (type I postural) → stretch
crossed.exercise: Stretch: grip the edge of the chair or bed to anchor the shoulder blade on the tight side; flex, side-bend and rotate the head AWAY from it, into the barrier - a stretch, not pain. Hold 15-20 s

crossed.name: Cervical erector spinae
crossed.pattern: Upper crossed · posterior · tight, facilitated (type I postural) → stretch
crossed.exercise: Stretched by the supine 'double chin' tuck - the same drill that strengthens the weak group at the front of the neck

crossed.name: Deep cervical flexors
crossed.pattern: Upper crossed · anterior · weak, inhibited (type II phasic) → strengthen
crossed.exercise: Strengthen: tuck the chin into a 'double chin' lying on a thin towel, or standing against a wall with a tennis ball under the chin as a cue - no head lift

crossed.name: Middle/lower trapezius & rhomboids
crossed.pattern: Upper crossed · posterior · weak, inhibited (type II phasic) → strengthen
crossed.exercise: Strengthen: back against a wall, elbows at shoulder height and bent 90°, rotate the forearms back to touch the wrists to the wall (hold 5 s, 8-20 reps); or prone, thumbs up, lift toward the ceiling

crossed.name: Latissimus dorsi
crossed.pattern: Upper crossed · posterior · weak, inhibited (type II phasic) → strengthen
crossed.exercise: Strengthen: back to the wall, start with both arms reaching straight overhead, then pull them down like a pull-down until the upper arms reach shoulder level, elbows bent 90°; repeat

crossed.name: Serratus anterior
crossed.pattern: Upper crossed · posterior · weak, inhibited (type II phasic) → strengthen

crossed.name: Iliopsoas
crossed.pattern: Lower crossed · anterior · tight, facilitated (type I postural) → stretch
crossed.exercise: Stretch: half-kneel with the opposite foot well forward (knee over ankle), shoulders back, and shift the pelvis forward; or lie supine at the bed's edge hugging one knee while the other leg hangs off. Hold 30-60 s

crossed.name: Rectus femoris
crossed.pattern: Lower crossed · anterior · tight, facilitated (type I postural) → stretch
crossed.exercise: Stretch: standing with one hand on the wall, pull the heel up toward the buttock (or rest the foot on a chair behind you if that is too hard). Hold 30-60 s

crossed.name: Adductor brevis
crossed.pattern: Lower crossed · anterior · tight, facilitated (type I postural) → stretch
crossed.exercise: Stretch: wide side lunge in the coronal plane - one knee bent, the other leg straight - shifting weight sideways until the groin pulls. Hold 30-60 s

crossed.name: Quadratus lumborum
crossed.pattern: Lower crossed · posterior · tight, facilitated (type I postural) → stretch
crossed.exercise: Stretch: seated on a bed with feet planted, side-bend the trunk to one side and hold up to 2 min; or stand, reach both arms overhead and lean to one side without leaning forward, 30-60 s

crossed.name: Thoracolumbar erector spinae
crossed.pattern: Lower crossed · posterior · tight, facilitated (type I postural) → stretch
crossed.exercise: Stretch into trunk flexion: lie supine and hug both knees to the chest, or kneel, reach the arms forward and sit the buttocks back onto the heels. Hold 30-60 s

crossed.name: Hamstrings
crossed.pattern: Lower crossed · posterior · tight, facilitated (type I postural) → stretch
crossed.exercise: Stretch: sit on the edge of a solid chair, one leg straight and one bent, hands on the bent knee, and lean toward the straight knee - felt mid-muscle, not at the sit bone or behind the knee. Hold ~45 s

crossed.name: Piriformis
crossed.pattern: Lower crossed · posterior · tight, facilitated (type I postural) → stretch
crossed.exercise: Stretch: seated, cross the affected ankle over the opposite thigh and lean forward with a straight back, head turned toward the crossed leg; or supine, pull the uncrossed thigh to the chest. Hold 30-60 s

crossed.name: Gastrocnemius-soleus complex
crossed.pattern: Lower crossed · posterior · tight, facilitated (type I postural) → stretch
crossed.exercise: Stretch: holding a counter, stand with the balls of the feet up on a 2x4 and the heels on the floor, knees straight. Hold 1-2 min

crossed.name: Rectus abdominis (abdominals)
crossed.pattern: Lower crossed · anterior · weak, inhibited (type II phasic) → strengthen
crossed.exercise: Strengthen: supine curl-up, lifting the head and upper back and reaching toward the knees; then a posterior pelvic tilt on exhalation for the lower fibers. 8-15 reps

crossed.name: Vastus lateralis, medialis & intermedius
crossed.pattern: Lower crossed · anterior · weak, inhibited (type II phasic) → strengthen
crossed.exercise: Strengthen: step up onto a bench straightening the knee, or stand on a step and bend that knee to lower the other heel and tap the floor (8-15 reps); or slide down a wall to a 90° squat with weight on the heels

crossed.name: Tibialis anterior
crossed.pattern: Lower crossed · anterior · weak, inhibited (type II phasic) → strengthen
crossed.exercise: Strengthen: holding a counter, rock back onto the heels and lift the toes as high as possible. 8-20 reps

crossed.name: Gluteus maximus
crossed.pattern: Lower crossed · posterior · weak, inhibited (type II phasic) → strengthen
crossed.exercise: Strengthen: hip extension - standing at a counter, swing the straight leg back without leaning forward, or lie prone and lift the straight leg. 12-15 reps each side

crossed.name: Gluteus medius & minimus
crossed.pattern: Lower crossed · posterior · weak, inhibited (type II phasic) → strengthen
crossed.exercise: Strengthen: side-lying straight-leg hip abduction to 30-40° with the top hand in front to stop rolling back; or stand on a step, standing knee locked straight, and hike the opposite hip. 8-15 reps

outlet.name: Interscalene (scalene) triangle
outlet.where: Anterior scalene in front, middle scalene behind, 1st rib as the floor. Brachial plexus trunks and the subclavian artery pass through; the subclavian vein runs in front of it
outlet.significance: Most common site of brachial plexus compression (neurogenic TOS); also where the subclavian artery is caught in arterial TOS

outlet.name: Costoclavicular space
outlet.where: Clavicle above, 1st rib below, subclavius in front, anterior scalene behind. Brachial plexus, subclavian artery AND subclavian vein all pass through
outlet.significance: Where the subclavian vein is most often compressed (venous TOS); narrowed by an elevated 1st rib or clavicular somatic dysfunction

outlet.name: Subcoracoid (pectoralis minor) space
outlet.where: Coracoid process above, pectoralis minor in front, upper ribs behind. Brachial plexus, axillary artery and axillary vein pass through
outlet.significance: Not strictly part of the thoracic outlet, yet compression here is almost as common as in the scalene triangle; a hypertonic front-wall muscle or rib dysfunction narrows it

outlet.name: Cervical rib
outlet.where: Congenital extra rib arising from C7 that crowds the brachial plexus and subclavian artery where they cross the 1st rib
outlet.significance: Seen on plain neck or chest films; it or an anomalous 1st rib underlies almost every case of arterial TOS

outlet.name: Anterior & middle scalenes
outlet.where: One arises from C3-C6, the other from C2-C7; both run down to insert on the 1st rib
outlet.significance: Hypertonicity or cervical somatic dysfunction narrows the triangle; their trigger points refer pain to the arm, chest and upper back and can mimic TOS

outlet.name: Rib 1 inhalation somatic dysfunction
outlet.where: 1st rib held up and resisting exhalation, raising the floor of the triangle and narrowing the gap under the clavicle
outlet.significance: A compressive cause of TOS symptoms; treated with muscle energy for the elevated 1st rib, with thoracic inlet release and cervical myofascial release

outlet.name: Adson's test
outlet.where: Examiner behind the patient stabilizes the shoulder and clavicle, extends the shoulder and monitors the radial pulse; board versions add neck extension, the head turned toward that side and a deep breath
outlet.significance: The most commonly used TOS test: a fading or absent pulse, or reproduced pain/paresthesia, implicates tight scalenes or an extra rib; false positives and negatives occur, so combine tests

outlet.name: Wright's (hyperabduction) test
outlet.where: The arm is passively raised fully overhead and externally rotated while the radial pulse is monitored
outlet.significance: Pulse loss or reproduced symptoms point to compression beneath the pectoralis minor, below the coracoid

outlet.name: Roos test (elevated arm stress test)
outlet.where: Both arms abducted 90° and externally rotated with the elbows bent 90°; the patient slowly opens and closes the hands for 3 minutes
outlet.significance: Positive if heaviness, pain or numbness forces the arms down early - a general provocative test for TOS

outlet.name: Costoclavicular (military brace) maneuver
outlet.where: The patient pulls the shoulders back and down with the chest pushed out, as if at attention, while the radial pulse is monitored
outlet.significance: Pulse loss or reproduced symptoms point to compression between the clavicle and the 1st rib

outlet.name: Spurling test
outlet.where: The neck is extended and side-bent/rotated toward the painful side, then pressed down from above
outlet.significance: Arm pain shooting down a dermatome points to cervical nerve root impingement - a mimic of (or companion to) TOS that must be excluded

outlet.name: Tinel's sign
outlet.where: Tapping over the ulnar groove at the elbow and over the median nerve at the wrist
outlet.significance: Tingling into the hand suggests a distal entrapment (ulnar at the elbow, carpal tunnel) that can mimic or coexist with TOS

outlet.name: Anterior scalene block
outlet.where: Local anesthetic injected into the front muscle wall of the triangle over the 1st rib (the muscle arising from C3-C6)
outlet.significance: Diagnostic and therapeutic: relief predicts a 94% good outcome after surgery, versus 50% in patients the injection fails to help

outlet.name: Conservative TOS care
outlet.where: Posture, stretching and strengthening rehab, OMT, activity changes and ergonomics, stress reduction, weight control, NSAIDs or muscle relaxants, and injections
outlet.significance: First line when there is no significant neurologic or vascular compromise; give an adequate 4-6 month trial with patient education and monitoring

outlet.name: 1st rib resection with scalenectomy
outlet.where: Surgical removal of the 1st rib, often with cutting or removing the neck muscles that form the triangle's front and back walls
outlet.significance: For neurogenic TOS that fails conservative care (excellent results in ~95%); often the initial management for arterial or venous TOS; risk includes brachial plexus injury

lymph.name: Terminal lymph drainage
lymph.fact: Emptying of the thoracic duct and right lymphatic trunk into the central veins; respiration produces about 35-60% of thoracic duct flow
lymph.clinical: Secure it first (Zink) with a good abdominothoracic venous pump - the real question is how effectively the patient breathes

lymph.name: Vascular lymph propulsion
lymph.fact: Vessel segments with smooth muscle and valves contract peristaltically on their own, generating enough pressure to move all lymph through the vessels
lymph.clinical: Thin, pliable vessels are easily compressed by tissue tension or somatic dysfunction at bottlenecks - clear the path of drainage before any lymph pump

lymph.name: Lymph formation
lymph.fact: Interstitial fluid must climb a small uphill hydrostatic gradient into the initial lymphatic, so external forces are needed; may be the limiting factor of total flow
lymph.clinical: The most effective way to increase lymph flow - fluid needs external forces such as alternating tissue movement and fluid fluctuation to enter

lymph.name: Lymphangion pacemaker coupling
lymph.fact: Electrical: spontaneous, rapid, spreads in both directions. Mechanical: stretch from filling triggers it - slow and one-way
lymph.clinical: Without filling there is no contraction at all, and frequency follows the perfusion rate - why a sympathomimetic 'lymph pill' never worked

lymph.name: Sympathetic innervation of lymphatics
lymph.fact: Alpha-receptor dominant; stimulation increases lymphangion contractility
lymph.clinical: Its effect on flow is small - researchers suggest it mainly modulates immune function rather than drainage

lymph.name: Cisterna chyli
lymph.fact: The bulb at the start of the thoracic duct, tucked under the thick diaphragmatic crura; the duct rises, then turns down into the veins like a siphon
lymph.clinical: Crural contraction squeezes it like a pump bulb; a locked-down diaphragm obstructs lymph from the whole abdomen and both legs - free the crura and upper lumbars

lymph.name: Venturi effect
lymph.fact: The thoracic duct enters at the junction of two central veins, which lowers the pressure lymph must drain against
lymph.clinical: One of the forces of terminal drainage, alongside negative intrathoracic pressure from breathing and the crural pump

lymph.name: Head & neck lymph
lymph.fact: Most of it must pass the tight jugulodigastric area just outside the C1 transverse process, between the mastoid process and the angle of the jaw
lymph.clinical: Found totally congested and dysfunctional in upper respiratory infections

lymph.name: Upper extremity & breast lymph
lymph.fact: Under the axillary fold (tightest at the pectoralis minor), then - even more critical - the space between the clavicle and the 1st rib
lymph.clinical: After axillary dissection with mastectomy, lymphedema usually appears 6-9 months later, once regenerated vessels fibrose shut

lymph.name: Lower extremity lymph
lymph.fact: Mostly the femoral triangle (beneath the inguinal ligament, over the iliopsoas), some behind the knee, then the diaphragm
lymph.clinical: For a swollen foot, palpate for congestion up the popliteal space, femoral triangle and inlet - the obstruction sits where the congestion stops

lymph.name: Heart & lung lymph
lymph.fact: Cardiac lymph drains out into the pericardium; both cardiac and pulmonary lymph then pass up through the mediastinal fascia
lymph.clinical: Acute obstruction: myocardial edema, hemorrhage, ischemia, lower contractility and output. Chronic: ventricular fibrosis and thickened mitral and tricuspid valves

lymph.name: Gut lymph
lymph.fact: Drains through the roots of the mesenteries, where they meet the posterior body wall
lymph.clinical: Mesenteric lymphatics are consistently obstructed in Crohn disease, and blocking intestinal lymphatics reproduces IBD-like bowel changes

lymph.name: Thoracic inlet
lymph.fact: Crowded junction of 1st rib, clavicle and cervicothoracic spine where the main duct and the head and neck lymph enter the veins
lymph.clinical: Dysfunction here can back lymph up in all directions - head and neck, arms, and the whole main duct

lymph.name: Anchoring filaments
lymph.fact: Tether initial lymphatics to the surrounding tissue, so alternating local movement changes vessel volume and draws fluid in

lymph.name: Overlapping endothelial cells
lymph.fact: Flap-like junctions let the ebb and flow of interstitial fluid fluctuation move fluid into the initial lymphatic

lymph.name: Arterial pulse
lymph.fact: Creates a small fluid fluctuation around the arterioles, where many lymphatics lie, and has been shown to form lymph there

lymph.name: Phasic skeletal muscle contraction
lymph.fact: Lymphatics pass between these tissues in the limbs, so their rhythmic squeezing promotes lymph formation

lymph.name: Respiratory excursions
lymph.fact: Form lymph in the lungs

lymph.name: Peristalsis & diaphragm motion
lymph.fact: Form lymph in the abdomen

lymph.name: Antigen delivery
lymph.fact: Lymph carries foreign material from the tissue to the nodes, where the immune response is initiated - especially important in infection

lymph.name: Inflammatory exudate
lymph.fact: Capillary permeability rises and protein floods the interstitium; local capillaries stagnate, so all circulation out of inflamed tissue is lymphatic

lymph.name: Resolution of inflammation
lymph.fact: Lymph carries mediators to the systemic circulation to be broken down, and removes the macrophages that have eaten the tissue-damaging neutrophils

lymph.name: Osmotic balance of the ECF
lymph.fact: The interstitium holds virtually no protein; lymphatics remove any that leaks out, preserving the protein gradient between capillary and tissue fluid

lymph.name: Lymphangiogenesis
lymph.fact: New lymph vessels grow in response to interstitial fluid flow; stasis instead reduces drainage and increases fibrosis

lymph.name: Lymph pump placement
lymph.fact: Over the swollen area itself, where lymph forms - a cuff over a sheep's calf did not drain its inflamed foot, but over the foot it did
lymph.clinical: Lymph flow rises with the rate and amplitude of compression (McGeown sheep studies)

lymph.name: Sequence of lymphatic treatment
lymph.fact: Terminal drainage first (breathing, thoracic inlet, diaphragm), then the bottlenecks along the vessels, and lymph formation with pump techniques last

lymph.name: Myocardial infarction with obstructed lymph
lymph.fact: Dogs with cardiac lymph tied off: larger, slower-healing necrosis that spreads into the ischemic zone and grows late. Separately, hyaluronidase kept lymphatics open and limited the damage

lymph.name: Pancreatitis
lymph.fact: In experimental attacks its enzymes appear in lymph at high levels; obliterating its lymph vessels can cause fatal necrotizing disease, and post-attack fibrosis may worsen later attacks

correlates.name: Neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome
correlates.presentation: A 32-year-old woman who stocks high shelves has 6 months of neck, trapezius and above-the-collarbone pain with occipital headaches; her hand tingles, worst in the 4th-5th fingers, when she reaches up. Pressing the side of her neck reproduces it; pulses normal.
correlates.mechanism: Brachial plexus (C5-T1), most often its lower part (C8-T1), compressed - usually between the anterior and middle scalenes over the 1st rib. Over 90% of cases
correlates.workup: Mostly clinical: history, provocative tests and the structural exam; EMG/NCS or MR neurography as needed. Relief after local anesthetic into the anterior scalene predicts a good surgical result (94% vs 50%)
correlates.management: 4-6 months of conservative care first: posture, stretching and strengthening, OMT to the neck, 1st rib, cervicothoracic junction and pectoralis minor, ergonomics, NSAIDs; if it fails, 1st rib resection with scalenectomy

correlates.name: Venous thoracic outlet syndrome (Paget-von Schroetter, effort thrombosis)
correlates.presentation: A 22-year-old competitive swimmer develops a heavy, swollen, bluish right arm during a week of hard training; the forearm tires within minutes of use, and dilated veins are visible over the shoulder and upper chest.
correlates.mechanism: Subclavian (or axillary) vein compressed between the clavicle and the 1st rib, often with clot forming in it. 10-15% of cases
correlates.workup: Duplex ultrasound or venography of the subclavian-axillary vein looking for narrowing or clot
correlates.management: Treat the clot (lytic therapy, heparin); surgical decompression is often the initial definitive treatment, with more than 95% of veins still open at 5 years

correlates.name: Arterial thoracic outlet syndrome
correlates.presentation: A 19-year-old pitcher has a pale, cold, aching right hand with tingling. BP is 20 mmHg lower in that arm and the radial pulse is faint at rest; the side of the neck is not tender, and arm positions do not change his symptoms.
correlates.mechanism: Subclavian (or axillary) artery compressed in the scalene triangle, almost always by an extra rib from C7 or an anomalous 1st rib. 2-5% of cases; can lead to aneurysm or thrombus
correlates.workup: Plain neck/chest films showing an extra rib; arteriography or angiography and hemodynamic testing for narrowing, aneurysm or clot
correlates.management: Usually surgical from the start (vascular surgeon): decompress by removing the offending rib and repair any aneurysm or clot

correlates.name: Upper crossed syndrome
correlates.presentation: A 30-year-old programmer has neck pain and headaches. From the side, his ear sits well in front of his shoulder, the shoulders roll forward, the thoracic curve is exaggerated, the lower neck is flexed and the upper neck extended.
correlates.mechanism: Tight type I postural muscles (pectorals, SCM, scalenes, upper trapezius, levator scapulae, cervical erector spinae) overpower inhibited type II phasic ones (deep neck flexors, mid-lower trapezius, rhomboids, latissimus, serratus anterior)
correlates.workup: Lying supine, he cannot lift his head off the table normally - the chin juts forward first; palpation and muscle testing find tight pectorals, upper trapezius and levator; imaging or EMG only if another cause is suspected
correlates.management: Postural education and OMT; stretch the pectorals, upper trapezius, levator scapulae, SCM and scalenes; strengthen deep neck flexors (chin tucks), mid trapezius and rhomboids (wrists-to-wall, prone thumbs-up) and latissimus (wall slides)

correlates.name: Lower crossed syndrome
correlates.presentation: A 45-year-old with chronic low back pain stands with the pelvis tipped forward, an exaggerated lumbar curve and a sagging belly; her feet roll inward, her knees angle toward each other, and on one leg the opposite hip drops.
correlates.mechanism: Tight type I muscles (iliopsoas and rectus femoris in front, lumbar erector spinae and quadratus lumborum behind) tilt the pelvis forward while inhibited abdominals and gluteals - especially gluteus medius - fail to counter them
correlates.workup: Observation, palpation and muscle testing: pelvis tipped forward over a deep low-back curve, flattened arches, knees angled inward; weak hip abduction, hip extension and trunk flexion; tight hip flexors and low-back extensors
correlates.management: Stretch the iliopsoas, rectus femoris, adductors, quadratus lumborum, erector spinae, hamstrings, piriformis and calves; strengthen the abdominals, vasti, tibialis anterior and gluteals; OMT and orthotics

correlates.name: Cervicogenic headache
correlates.presentation: A 55-year-old with years of neck stiffness has recurring pain at the back of the head that builds with sustained neck postures; neurologic exam is normal, and plain films show only age-related degenerative change.
correlates.mechanism: Most often the C2/3 zygapophyseal (facet) joint, referring mainly to the occiput; C1/2 and C3/4 come next (C1/2 refers higher). Upper-neck pain reaches the head through the trigeminal nucleus caudalis
correlates.workup: A diagnostic medial branch block of the dorsal ramus at C2/3 that abolishes the pain; degenerative change on X-ray or MRI alone does not prove the pain source
correlates.management: Radiofrequency ablation of the medial branches after a positive block (nerves regrow over a year or more; repeatable); months of posture work, stretching, fascial release and manipulation; occipital nerve blocks give only brief relief
